496: The appellants were convicted and sentenced to death under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code. They challenged the convictions on the ground that they had been acquitted by the Sessions Judge in a previous trial and that their conviction was illegal as they did not have been properly recorded. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the accused could be released only on the basis of the evidence adduced against him and that the sentence awarded to them should be commuted to imprisonment for life. It is well settled that where the accused has been acquitted by a single judge of the same offence, it cannot be said that he must be given the benefit of any particular length of time or length of time. In such a case, the accused may be tried again for all offences which are committed at the earliest stage. But if the accused does not appear before the court, he can be tried again on the basis Of the evidence adduced in the case. If the accused makes an application for bail the fact that he has not appeared before the court would not have held him to have been duly appointed, the accused will be entitled to bail unless he made an application for such bail.

The Army Rules also provided that on acquittal by Court Martial, an Officer shall be called upon to submit his explanation and defence. In the petition for special leave to appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the Army Rules, 1959, which were framed in exer cise of the powers conferred by section 191(2)(a), as amended by the Defence of india Amendment Act, 1964, had no application to the case; (ii) the Army Rule, 1959, did not provide for dismissal from service, and (iii) the Army rules could not have been made applicable to the case because they were not inconsistent with the provisions of the Army Rules. But the power under section 19 is an independent power. It cannot be said that the Army Rules were not inconsistent therewith. [951 E F] (b) The Army Act is a self contained provision. It has nothing to do with the powers of the Central Government or the Central Government under section 19 of the Act. The Army Rule, therefore, must be deemed to be void. 7130: The appellants are the legal representatives of the deceased plaintiff in a suit for declaration and an injunction to restrain the defendants from dispossessing him from the property known as 'Palmar Oiteral do Predi Martins who died pendente lite. He had on October 26, 1967 instituted a suit No. 114/74 on May 6, 1968 for a declaration and an interim injunction to restrain defendant No. 2 from dispossessed him from the suit property. The suit was dismissed on May 6. 1969 on the ground that the plaintiff was not in possession of the suit property and since he had not been dispossessed,in accordance with law the defen dants who were mere trespassers were liable to be evicted. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiff had failed to prove his case that he was forcibly dispossessed by defendant No. 1 in collusion with defendant No.2 and that the suit was barred on the principle of res judicata and/or constructive res judicata as found in Order 2 Rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1973, averred that on the expiry of the lease at the end of December, 1967 the lease stood terminated by efflux of time and defendant No. 3 was, therefore, entitled to let out the property to defendant No.1 and hence the latter was in lawful possession of the said property. The Trial Court held that the plaintiff being in lawful possession was not entitled to evict the defendant No. I and consequently the suit was decreed ex parte. On appeal the High Court reversed this decision. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the suit was not barred on the principles of res judicata; (ii) the suit having been filed after the expiry of six months of the expiry of tenancy, the suit was hit by article 14 of the Constitution; (iii) the suit being one for a declaration that the plaintiff is not in possession or has become absolute owner of the property, the suit should have been dismissed; (iv) the suit must fail because the suit was filed after the expiration of six months from the date of the expiry, and the suit was bad as barred by article 14; and (v) the suit could not be proceeded with under section 5

The Union filed an application before the Conciliation Officer for referring to the conciliation proceedings to the Industrial Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the conciliation proceedings had continued for a period of more than 14 days as from January 17, 1952, further proceedings for conciliation were illegal and therefore the respondent could not be convicted under section 31(1) Of the Act. The appellants contended that the conciliation proceeding should be held to terminate when the report under section 12(6) of the Act was made by the Conciliation Officer within two months of the commencement of the conciliation proceedings or within such shorter period fixed by the appropriate Government. Held, that the provisions of section 12( 6) of the , are applicable to the facts of the case and they are not intended to operate as res judicata in any proceedings which can be brought under the Act. It is only where the report under s.12(6) is made by the conciliation officer within one month of the commencement thereof that the report is made by him within that time, and if for some reason the Conciliation Officer delays the submission of his report, the matter would have to be referred to the Industrial tribunal.

1778: The appellant, a private limited company, entered into an agreement with the respondent company for supply of certain work to its workmen. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the award on the ground that the wages prescribed by the award could not be included. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the definition of wages contained in section 2(v) of the Industrial Disputes (Amendment and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1976 did not apply to the case because the wages prescribed under the award could be treated as wages under section 2(i)(vi). In appeal to this Court it was contended that before the High court was justified in dismissing the petition, it was contended: (1) that the provisions of the award are not applicable to the case; (2) that the award itself is a contract between the parties, because that, in substance, is the effect of industrial adjudication; (3) that the very purpose for which industrial adjudication has been given the peculiar authority and right of making new contracts between employers and workmen makes it reasonable to think that even though the period of operation of the award and the period for which it remains binding on the parties may sharer, it must be held that the award cannot fall within the definition of "workman" under section 2 (vi) of Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The definition of wages in section 2 (vii) of the , does not make it clear that the term "workman ' includes a person who has been employed in connection with or in connection with the affairs of the employer. [869 C] 2. The definition is wide enough to include all matters covered by the contract between the employer and the employees. It is well settled that unless there is anything repugnant in the subject matter of the contract, the word "workman " means a person who is engaged in the business of the employer and whose employment is incidental to it. The definition does not make such a distinction. The definition further provides that the definition shall have reference to the totality of the work man
5471: The appellant was a company carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling houses in the city of Calcutta. In order to secure accommodation, the respondent company had obtained possession of certain premises under cls. (a) to (b) of section 630 of the Indian Penal Code and for wrongful withholding of property (1) if any officer or employee of a company (a) wrongfully obtained possession of any property of a company; or (b) having any such property in his possession wrongfully obtained possession by a present officer or employee. The respondent company filed a complaint against the appellant alleging that he had been wrongly obtained possession of the property under cl. (a), (c) of section 528 of the Indian Criminal Procedure Code, and that the trial court had no jurisdiction to try the offence. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the provisions contained in sub s.(1) of section 430 of the Code of Criminal Procedure were not applicable to the case. On appeal by special leave, Held:(i) that the words "any person" used in sub section (1) of Section 630 of Indian Penal Code must be interpreted to mean not only the present officers and employees of a company but also to include past officers and employees who have been granted protection from criminal proceedings. The word "any person " in section 630 means an officer or employee who has been granted protection to be given protection to the extent of the benefit of the Act. The words "any such property" in section 631(l)(b) are wide enough to cover every person who is entitled to get protection under the Act. It cannot be said that the words 'any such property ' in section 629(1) of the Code should be construed to mean not merely the present officers or employee of the company but also the present officers as such persons and employees of the company. The Corporation also asserted that the petitioners were paid the same pay as per the revised scales of pay and other conditions of service. 660: The appellant, a Hindu widow and her daughter, executed a will in favour of the respondent. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed this decision. HELD : (i) The will was not proved to be the last will and the will was therefore not a genuine or valid. [850 D] (ii) There is no doubt that the will was a genuine one. But if it had been found that the testator was not in a sound disposing state of mind, he could not have made a will in respect of any of the items which were in dispute. It would be sufficient if the testator himself had made a will. If the testator himself made a will, there was no necessity for it. [851 C] (iii) The will must be held to be an absolute one. The will did neither show that the testator intended to sell the property to anyone else nor did it contain any provision to the contrary. [855 E] (v) The will merely stated that the testator had made a gift of the property to another person. The will also contained a recital that the testator wanted to sell the properties to anyone

2052: The respondents were employed in banks which were not governed by the Sastry award as modified by the Labour Appellate Tribunal. The workmen contended that they were not entitled either to the same scale or higher scales of pay provided by the Desai award. Held, that the workmen were entitled to all the benefits conferred on them under the Desai Award. The workmen were not entitled even to the same allowance as they were not similarly situated as they were also similarly situated. 5266: The appellants were the owners of a plot in the State of West Bengal. They had constructed a building and vacant land in the eight acre plot of land.
